I'm 65 years old and I've farmed these 6 mu in Quzhou County my whole life. My father farmed this land before me. I know every plot, where the soil is heavier and where it dries out faster. I finished middle school, which was more than most of my generation, but honestly it's the forty years in the field that taught me what works. I don't chase new trends — I grow what the land and the market here on the North China Plain reliably reward.

Last October I sowed winter wheat on all six mu, like I always do. The start of the growing season means the wheat is greening up now, and my main job is managing it through to the June harvest, then immediately putting in summer maize. This wheat-maize rotation is the backbone of my farm. I've tried other things over the years, but nothing pays as steadily as this pair, and at my age I don't have the strength or the risk appetite to experiment. The county grain station buys wheat, and there's always a market for corn — either the state purchase or the local feed mill.

For the wheat, I use improved seeds from the county supply store. They're not the newest hybrids, but they're proven here. I'll topdress nitrogen when the wheat joints in spring — that's the critical window. Phosphorus and potassium went on as base fertilizer before sowing, but I count the total for the season. I'll irrigate four times: the return-green water, jointing water, heading water, and one grain-filling water if the sky stays dry, which it usually does here in spring. I rotary-tilled before sowing last autumn, and I'll do the same for the maize after harvest. Three rounds of pesticide — a herbicide early, then fungicide and insecticide when the weather turns humid.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I'll plant hybrid summer maize immediately. Timing is everything — every day of delay costs yield. The maize gets slightly less fertilizer than the wheat because the growing season is shorter, but it still needs plenty of nitrogen to bulk up. I'll irrigate three times: at sowing if the soil is dry, at the big-flare stage, and at filling. Two pesticide sprays — one for weeds, one for the borers that always come in August. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 480 jin per mu of wheat and 550 jin per mu of corn. That feeds my family and leaves enough to sell.
